paper_title: eDIAR: Training-Free Open-Speaker Streaming Diarization for Long Meetings and Large Archives via e-means

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Meetings last up to an hour, and nobody knows in advance how many people will speak. Neural diarizers with a fixed number of output slots, such as Streaming Sortformer and Nemotron-3, are accurate and run online, but they cannot name more speakers than they have slots. We remove this limit without retraining. The slot head keeps deciding who is active and when speech overlaps, and speaker embeddings are clustered inside a single slot, with the official e-means algorithm, only after every slot has been used. In the streaming system, re-clustering is confined to a bounded window, labels are revised for a few seconds, and identities are anchored to the slots of the head. The resulting system has no limit on the number of speakers and stays accurate when speakers outnumber the slots, where fixed-slot models break down. On meetings that grow to an hour it stays far more accurate than Streaming Sortformer, which accumulates errors, and its cost per update does not grow with the meeting. The same recipe turns the four-slot Streaming Sortformer into an open-speaker system. Across recordings, e-means makes it affordable to link the speakers of a large archive frame by frame, a task that arises when conversational corpora are prepared, and it reaches the clustering quality of Lloyd's $k$-means several times faster. The method needs little tuning, and e-means runs with its default recipe from a few hundred to more than a million embeddings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Speaker diarization answers who spoke when. It is first step of meeting transcription and is also needed to prepare multi-turn conversational audio at scale (Jung et al., 2026), and meeting assistant has to answer it while the meeting is still going on. End-to-end diarizers with fixed number of output channels (Fujita et al., 2019) are well suited to this. They resolve the speaker permutation by arrival order and stream through speaker cache and FIFO queue (Park et al., 2024; Medennikov et al., 2025, 2026). Their weakness is capacity. four-slot model cannot output fifth speaker, and an eight-slot model has to reuse slot once ninth person talks. Clustering pipelines (Bredin, 2023) have no such cap, but they decide identity from short and noisy embeddings alone, and their simple online forms commit to early decisions that they cannot repair later. These two weaknesses are hit by different situations. Slot capacity is hit by large gatherings, whereas the drift of an online clusterer is hit by long ones, and real meetings are long. system that is to be used for whole meeting needs the identity stability of the slot head together with the unbounded speaker count of clustering. We combine the two with as little machinery as possible. The slot head is trusted for activity, for overlap and, as long as free slot exists, for identity. Clustering is used only for the one decision fixed-slot head cannot make, namely that single slot hosts several voices. Since head gives new speaker an unused slot first, we split slot only when all slots have been used, which we call capacity-aware splitting. The splitting uses the official e-means algorithm (Bessa et al., 2026) in its spherical form. The recipe is not tied to one model, and it turns the four-slot Streaming Sortformer into an open-speaker system as well. The same reasoning extends beyond single recording. Meeting series, podcast archives and corpora collected for conversational speech models contain the same people many times, and the speakers found in each session must be linked to one identity across the whole archive. That is clustering problem with millions of embeddings and thousands of clusters, which is exactly the regime for which e-means was designed. There it matches the loss of Lloyds algorithm in fraction of the passes and of the time, and this makes it affordable to link every frame rather than one centroid per local speaker, the more accurate choice. In short, simple addition to an existing slot model keeps everything that model already does well, namely its decisions about activity and overlap, its accuracy on meetings that fit into its slots and its latency, and it adds four properties the model lacks: an unlimited number of speakers, robustness on long meetings, speaker linking across recordings and low, constant compute cost. No retraining is needed, and the addition is clustering step of few hundred lines on top of the outputs of the slot model. Our system offers four practical advantages, summarised in Figure 1 and demonstrated in turn. No cap on the number of speakers. Any slot head becomes open-speaker without retraining, shown for Nemotron-3 and Streaming Sortformer (Section 6.1). Robust as meetings grow longer. Boundedwindow re-clustering and slot-anchored identities keep the error well below that of Streaming Sortformer on hour-long meetings and ahead of the slot head (Section 6.3). Linking speakers across recordings. Framelevel linking with e-means finds the same person across an archive of more than thousand speakers (Section 6.4). Low and constant compute. The cost per update does not grow with the meeting, and e-means clusters million frames in seconds on CPU (Section 6.5).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Clustering pipelines. Classical diarization extracts speaker embeddings from short windows and clusters them. Embeddings range from LSTMbased d-vectors (Wang et al., 2017) to ECAPATDNN (Desplanques et al., 2020) and WeSpeaker ResNets (Wang et al., 2023), and clustering from agglomerative and spectral methods to Bayesian HMMs (Landini et al., 2020). pyannote 3.1 (Bredin, 2023; Plaquet and Bredin, 2023) combines segmentation model with such embeddings and clustering. Supervised alternatives replace the clustering step by recurrent model (Zhang et al., 2018) or by neural clusterer (Li et al., 2019). Park et al. (2021) survey the field. Online variants commit to early decisions, and the classical online and minibatch k-means (MacQueen, 1967; Sculley, 2010; Lloyd, 1982; Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007) serve as our baselines. End-to-end and hybrid diarization. EEND (Fujita et al., 2019) predicts speaker activity directly, with an attractor module for flexible number of speakers (Horiguchi et al., 2020). Online versions use speaker-tracing buffer (Xue et al., 2020), handle overlap and flexible speaker count while streaming (Xue et al., 2021), or use global and local attractors for an unlimited number of speakers (Horiguchi et al., 2022). Hybrids combine EEND with clustering to cope with many speakers (Kinoshita et al., 2020, 2021), and target-speaker VAD refines activity given speaker profiles (Medennikov et al., 2020). NeMos multi-scale diarization decoder weights embeddings of several window scales (Park et al., 2022). Our system is hybrid in the same spirit, with one difference: clustering is confined to one slot and only after capacity is exhausted. Fixed-slot neural diarization. Sortformer (Park et al., 2024) orders output channels by speaker arrival time. Streaming Sortformer (Medennikov et al., 2025) adds an Arrival-Order Speaker Cache and FIFO queue. Nemotron-3 Diarization (Medennikov et al., 2026) supports up to eight speakers and several input-buffer latencies, and we use its released streaming API as the slot head. Speaker linking. Linking the speakers of many recordings to common identities has been studied as speaker linking in large data sets (van Leeuwen, 2010) and as joint diarization and linking of large corpora (Ferràs and Bourlard, 2012), usually by agglomerative clustering of one model per local speaker. We revisit it with clustering at the level of frames, which requires an engine that scales to millions of points and thousands of clusters. e-means. e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) replaces the iterations of Lloyds algorithm by mini-batch updates of an exponential moving average, as used for codebooks in vector-quantised autoencoders (Van Den Oord et al., 2017), and is released in Faiss (Douze et al., 2024), with batch size and step size taken from fitted scaling laws. Its selling point is that it reaches given clustering loss in far fewer passes over the data. It needs fixed number of clusters, so choosing it is part of our contribution. Figure 1: eDIAR at glance. Streaming at 1.04 s. (a) DER against the number of speakers, from two to twenty, on LibriSpeech-OpenSpk conversations, compared with the two fixed-slot models; the dotted lines mark four and eight slots. (b) DER of six one-hour meetings with 12 to 20 speakers (LibriSpeech-OpenSpk utterances, speakers joining over time), scored on their first 15, 30 and 45 minutes. (c) Linking the speakers of 1,248 sessions with 1,251 VoxCeleb1 speakers across recordings: archive DER against clustering time at the level of 1.16 million frames; numbers next to the markers are passes over the data. (d) Processing time per update over the same long recordings, for our bounded 90 window and for re-clustering the whole history, with the real-time budget of one 0.72 chunk.

sections.title: 4 Streaming System
sections.content: Slot head. The Nemotron-3 streaming API is called chunk by chunk and carries its own speaker cache and FIFO. We use its low-latency mode with 1.04 input buffer and its very-low-latency mode with 0.64 s. Causal embeddings. Mel features are normalised with cumulative mean, and the ResNet runs on short blocks with little history and lookahead. causal embedding pools the window that ends at the current frame and is available immediately. The centred embedding, which is the original pooling window, becomes available 0.72 later and replaces the causal one when labels are recomputed. This retroactive correction matters when speakers change quickly. Online clustering with revision. After each chunk, the slot-conditioned clustering is re-run on the last 90 s. Labels become visible as soon as they are computed (as first emitted) and may be revised by later re-clustering until they are 10 old; older labels are frozen. Slot-anchored speaker ids. permanent id is tied to the slot, because the speaker cache keeps slot bound to one speaker over time. An unsplit slot keeps its id. The sub-clusters of split slot are matched to the ids already registered for that slot by centroid cosine with the Hungarian algorithm, and unmatched ones receive new ids. Once all slots have been used, splitting stays enabled for the rest of the session. Anchoring ids to slots keeps them stable over long meetings.

sections.title: 5 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Data. VoxConverse (Chung et al., 2020) with 44 sessions, 15 with 14, 15 with 58 and 14 with 9+ speakers, cut to the first 480 s; AMI (Carletta et al., 2005) ihm-mix test with 16 meetings of 420 s; ICSI (Janin et al., 2003) test with 15 meetings of 420 s; and LibriSpeech-OpenSpk, 18 synthetic conversations of {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12} speakers, three each, built from LibriSpeech (Panayotov et al., 2015) test-clean with 0.120.28 pauses and 0.35 overlap every seventh turn. Within every corpus, alternate sessions form dev half used for all tuning and held-out half. Appendix describes every evaluation set and how it was built. Metrics. DER with 0.25 collar and overlap scored with pyannote.metrics; hypotheses are merged across gaps shorter than 0.16 s. Speakercount accuracy, SCA, is the share of sessions with the exact number of speakers, and MAE is the mean absolute error of the count. cpWER is the concatenated-permutation WER obtained when the reference words are tagged by the systems speakers, using oracle transcripts, so it isolates diarization errors. Systems. We compare against the official Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1 (Medennikov et al., 2025) in its low-latency and its 30.4 configuration, the Nemotron-3 head alone, and pyannote 3.1 with default settings. Three clustering baselines operate on the same embeddings as our system, concatenated with the slot posteriors, behind simple activity gate: leaderfollower, mini-batch k-means and Lloyd k-means++. Leaderfollower (MacQueen, 1967) processes embeddings in time order, assigns each to the nearest cluster when the cosine similarity is high enough, otherwise opens new cluster, updates the cluster mean, and never revises an earlier label. Its results are reported in Appendix B.3. In the non-streaming setting the head runs in its 30.4 configuration and clustering sees all embeddings of the session. In the streaming setting audio is fed in 100 ms chunks, as in the live server, and clustering baselines get streaming embeddings. Inference runs on one NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 24 GiB of shared server with two Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPUs of 80 threads, and all clustering runs on the CPU.

sections.title: 6.1 No cap on the number of speakers
sections.content: Tables 1 and 2 compare the systems on all four corpora. Our system gives the lowest error on VoxConverse in both settings, on ICSI in both settings and on LibriSpeech in the non-streaming setting, and it estimates the number of speakers correctly in more sessions than any other system on almost every corpus. The pattern behind these numbers is simple. Wherever session has more speakers than the head has slots, the fixed-slot models must merge people, and our system does not. Where meetings have few speakers, as in AMI and ICSI, our clustering is rarely invoked and the system keeps the accuracy of its head, so the extra capacity comes for free. Bootstrap intervals in Table 3 confirm the gains over the head and Streaming Sortformer on corpora with many speakers. The capacity is not property of Nemotron-3. The method only needs per-frame slot posteriors and speaker embeddings, so we also place it on the four-slot Streaming Sortformer, see Table 4. On VoxConverse and LibriSpeech, where most sessions have more than four speakers, our clustering removes most of the error that the speaker limit of Sortformer causes. Any slot head can thus be made open-speaker in the same way.

sections.title: 6.2 Robust when speakers outnumber slots
sections.content: Figure 1a follows the error as the number of speakers grows. Both fixed-slot models break down at their capacity, the four-slot Sortformer beyond four speakers and the eight-slot head beyond eight. Our system follows the head while free slots remain and degrades only gradually once they are used up. At twenty speakers its error is about two thirds of that of the head and about half of that of Sortformer. Appendix B.1 adds offline pyannote 3.1. The ablation in Table 14 attributes this to the two design choices, splitting slot and doing so only when capacity is exhausted. The same ordering holds when much of the speech overlaps: with up to twelve speakers and forty percent overlap, our system stays ahead of both fixed-slot models beyond the slot count, see Appendix B.8.

sections.title: 6.3 Robust as meetings grow longer
sections.content: Figure 1b scores six one-hour meetings of 12 to 20 speakers, built from LibriSpeech-OpenSpk utterances with speakers joining over time, on the first 15, 30 and 45 minutes. Streaming Sortformer collapses, from 23 % after 15 minutes to 57 % after 45. Our system and the Nemotron-3 head stay far below it, and ours is ahead of the head at every length and for all three speaker counts, by about half point. The gain is small because within the 90 window rarely more than eight speakers are active, so the slots mostly suffice. Appendix B.2 adds three-hour ICSI recordings, where our system behaves like the head, and harder setting with short turns in which our error grows and passes that of the head after half an hour. Table 5 confirms this on all real sessions at full length, up to an hour: our system is the best or within point of the best on every corpus, which Streaming Sortformer does not achieve. Appendix B.3 shows how much online clustering degrades. The robustness is structural. Re-clustering is confined to bounded window, so an early mistake cannot spread through the whole meeting, and identities are tied to the slots of the head, which the speaker cache keeps bound to the same person. running centroid bank without revision, by contrast, drifts, and every early mistake travels to the end of the meeting. system that looks good on short clip can be the wrong choice for meeting.

sections.title: 6.4 Linking speakers across recordings
sections.content: A series of meetings, podcast archive or corpus prepared for training conversational speech models (Jung et al., 2026) contains the same people many times, and the speakers found in each session have to be linked to identities that hold across the whole archive (van Leeuwen, 2010; Ferràs and Bourlard, 2012). This is hard task for two reasons. The same voice has to be recognised across changes of channel, room and microphone, and the clustering problem is large, with hundreds of thousands to millions of embeddings and as many clusters as there are people. The second is exactly the regime e-means was designed for. Setup. We built an archive from VoxCeleb1 (Nagrani et al., 2017), whose speakers do not occur in the VoxCeleb2 data on which the embedding model was trained (Chung et al., 2018). sections.title: 6.5 Low and constant compute
sections.content: The streaming system does the same amount of work at every update, because it only re-clusters bounded window. Figure 1d shows that the time per update stays flat over the three-hour recordings, whereas re-clustering the whole history grows steadily toward the real-time budget. The persession clustering problems are small, few hundred embeddings and at most four clusters, so the clustering step costs milliseconds. Across an archive, e-means clusters million frames in seconds. Latency. The input buffer of Nemotron-3 is 1.04 in low latency mode and 0.64 in very low latency mode. The ResNet runs in parallel with the head and needs only 0.2 to 0.5 of look-ahead, which we measured by replacing the audio after time t0 with noise and finding the earliest affected frame. It therefore adds no latency. In total this is about 75 GFLOP per second of audio. We did not count the FLOPs of Streaming Sortformer. GPU, CPU and memory. With BLAS threads limited to 4, the server process held 850 MiB of GPU memory. The average GPU utilisation was 1.4 % for 4 speakers and 2.1 % for 10 speakers, with peaks of 7 to 8 %. The process used on average 0.33 and 1.13 CPU cores and constant 1.9 GiB of resident memory. The server time per update was 56 ms for 4 speakers, and 188 ms on average and 346 ms at the 95th percentile for 10 speakers. These are real-time factors of 0.074 and 0.25, since the chunk period is 720 ms. Over all 93 benchmark sessions, fed as fast as possible on the shared host, the mean real-time factor was 0.10 with 95th percentile of 0.24. Streaming Sortformer, run with NeMo at batch size 1 under the same conditions, had 0.07. On the longest recording, 3.2 of ICSI, the streaming system peaked at 0.43 GiB of GPU memory, of which 0.40 GiB are the weights, whereas Streaming Sortformer reached 9.6 GiB. Both held about 3.8 GiB of resident CPU memory. Frame-level archive linking of 1.16 frames with = 1,251 on 16 threads peaked at 4.5 GiB and took 12.2 with e-means after 5 epochs and 46.5 with Lloyds algorithm after 25 iterations.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Fixed-slot diarizers cannot name more speakers than they have slots, and online clustering drifts as meeting grows. Without retraining, we let the slot head decide activity and overlap, split slot only once every slot is in use, and bound error and cost over hours with fixed window and slot-anchored identities. The result has no speaker cap, carries over to Streaming Sortformer, and, with e-means, links an archives speakers frame by frame several times faster than Lloyds algorithm. It keeps the accuracy of the head on meetings that fit into the slots and, at twenty speakers, lowers the error from 66 to 44 % for Nemotron-3 and from 81 to 44 % for Sortformer. The gain on long meetings is modest, and many speakers in rapid turns remain hard.

sections.title: 8 Limitations
sections.content: Data. The real corpora are small, and the open-speaker and archive benchmarks are built from read or interview speech, so they complement but do not replace large real meeting collections. Tuning. The thresholds were set on the dev half of the same corpora, and the held-out half serves as check. Long, speaker-rich meetings. When more than few speakers talk in rapid alternation for an hour, the error of our system grows with the length and can exceed that of the slot head (Appendix B.2). Archive linking. The number of archive speakers is given to the clustering. Scope. All recordings are in English, and we did not evaluate far-field rooms.

sections.title: Ethics
sections.content: The live demo processes microphone audio in server memory only and stores nothing; it runs one session at time. Speaker ids are anonymous and are not linked to identities. Linking speakers across an archive can re-identify person across recordings. We use it only on public research corpus, and any deployment on real recordings needs the consent of the people recorded.

sections.title: A Evaluation Data
sections.content: Table 8 summarises the evaluation sets. All audio is resampled to 16 kHz mono. Within every real corpus, alternate sessions form dev half, which was used for all tuning, and held-out half. VoxConverse. VoxConverse (Chung et al., 2020) consists of multi-speaker clips of YouTube videos such as news, debates and talk shows, with speakers who often talk over background music or each other. We take the recordings of the first shard of the development set and the first two shards of the test set in the release on the Hugging Face Hub, group them by the number of speakers in the full recording, and keep, in the order of the release, the first fifteen recordings with one to four speakers, the first fifteen with five to eight and all fourteen with nine or more speakers in these shards, 44 recordings in total. For the main tables each recording is cut to its first 480 s, which leaves between one and seventeen speakers per session. The full-length evaluation uses the same 44 recordings uncut, with up to twenty-one speakers and up to twenty minutes. AMI. The AMI Meeting Corpus (Carletta et al., 2005) contains meetings of four participants, most of them in design scenario in which the group plays product-development team. We use the sixteen meetings of the standard test split in the ihm-mix condition, mix of the individual headset microphones, together with the word-level transcripts and speaker labels of the release on the Hugging Face Hub. One meeting has three speakers and the others four. The main tables use the first 420 of each meeting, and the full-length evaluation uses the complete meetings of fourteen to fifty minutes. Word timestamps from the transcripts allow cpWER with oracle transcripts. ICSI. The ICSI Meeting Corpus (Janin et al., 2003) records natural, unscripted research meetings of group at the International Computer Science Institute. They have more participants than AMI, more spontaneous interaction and the largest share of overlapped speech among our corpora. We use the fifteen test meetings of the release on the Hugging Face Hub, cut to 420 for the main tables, which leaves four to seven speakers per session, and complete for the full-length evaluation, with forty-four to eighty-six minutes and up to ten speakers. ICSI speaker identifiers are global, because the same research group meets repeatedly, which we use for the long recordings below. LibriSpeech-OpenSpk. LibriSpeech (Panayotov et al., 2015) is corpus of read audiobooks for speech recognition, in which every utterance has single speaker. It has no conversations, so we build them from the test-clean subset, which contains forty speakers who do not occur in the training subsets. For conversation with speakers we draw distinct speakers at random among those with at least six utterances. The conversation has three rounds, and in each round every speaker takes one turn, in fresh random order, so that each speaker talks three times and turns of different speakers alternate. turn is one utterance of that speaker, truncated to its first 4.5 s, and different turns of speaker use different utterances. Consecutive turns are separated by pause drawn uniformly between 0.12 and 0.28 s, and every seventh turn starts 0.35 before the previous one ends, which creates short overlap. The reference segments are the exact positions of the turns, so the reference is free of annotation noise. The transcript of turn is the LibriSpeech transcript, shortened in proportion to the truncation, and its words are spread evenly over the turn to give the word timestamps that cpWER needs. The benchmark of the main tables has three conversations for each {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}. For the evaluation on unseen data we built ten more conversations for each of these with different random seed, and for the many-speaker evaluation five conversations for each {14, 16, 18, 20} with third seed. Speaker identities can repeat between these sets because test-clean has only forty speakers, but the speaker subsets, utterances and turn orders are new. Overlap-controlled conversations. For the analysis of many speakers with heavy overlap we use the same construction with five rounds and {6, 8, 10, 12}, and we let turn start before the previous turn ends with probability {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75}, by 1.0 to 2.5 s. Three conversations per combination give 48 conversations whose share of overlapped speech ranges from zero to about forty percent. ICSI meeting days. To evaluate recordings longer than any single meeting, we join three consecutive ICSI test meetings with two seconds of silence into one recording, which gives five recordings of 2.6 to 3.2 hours with nine to eleven speakers each. Because ICSI speaker identifiers are global, person who attends several of the joined meetings keeps one identity in the reference, as in day of back-to-back meetings of the same group. VoxCeleb1 archive. The archive for speaker linking is built from VoxCeleb1 (Nagrani et al., Figure 3: Figure 1a and restricted to up to 12 speakers and 60 minutes, with offline pyannote 3.1 added; hollow markers are the Nemotron-3 head. Figure 4: (a) Five ICSI days of up to three hours (hollow markers: Nemotron-3 head, almost identical to ours). (b) One-hour meetings with 12 to 20 speakers, short turns, all speakers present from the start. 2017), interviews of 1,251 celebrities extracted from YouTube videos, whose speakers are disjoint from the VoxCeleb2 data on which the embedding model was trained (Chung et al., 2018). Every speaker takes part in six sessions. For each of six rounds the speakers are shuffled and grouped into sessions of six, with the few remaining speakers added to sessions of seven. Within session speaker takes three turns, all from one video, and the six sessions of speaker use six different videos where the speaker has that many. Turns are truncated, separated and overlapped as in LibriSpeechOpenSpk. The result is 1,248 sessions with 29 hours of audio.

sections.content: B.1 Comparison with pyannote 3.1 Figure 3 adds pyannote 3.1 with default settings to the two comparisons of Figure 1, restricted to the ranges where our system is ahead. pyannote 3.1 is an offline system: for the long recordings it is rerun from scratch on every prefix, and for the conversations it sees the whole session. Up to twelve speakers our system has lower error than pyannote 3.1 at every speaker count (a), and on the long meetings it is lower on the first 15 to 60 minutes (b). Beyond that the picture changes: on the full 2.5 recordings pyannote 3.1 reaches about 29 % against our 31 %, and from sixteen speakers on its error (about 34 %) is below ours (41 to 44 %), since it is not limited by slots and sees all the audio. Our system is streaming, with bounded cost per update. 15 to 150 minutes. The speakers of each day fit into the eight slots, so our system is within 0.1 points of the Nemotron-3 head, and both stay far below Streaming Sortformer. Figure 4b is harder setting: six one-hour meetings of 12 to 20 speakers who are all present from the start and speak in short turns of 2 to 4 seconds. Our system is ahead of the head after 15 minutes (45 against 51 %), but its error grows with the length of the meeting and exceeds that of the head from 30 minutes on (60 against 52 % after an hour), while Streaming Sortformer stays at 75 to 77 %. We read this as limit of the bounded window: with many speakers talking in rapid alternation the window holds only few turns of each, and identities that the head has already assigned to slots are not corrected over time.
